I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite challenging, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses. It feels surreal to have come so far from my intro classes to now tackling complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics.
store.1: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite challenging, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses. It feels surreal to have come so far from my intro classes to now tackling complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics.
store.2: My favorite class this semester is Advanced Algorithms. I'm fascinated by the theory behind real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or handling huge datasets efficiently. The class covers dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems, which can be mind-bending. However, our professor's intuitive explanations make these complex concepts more accessible. She presents seemingly impossible problems and shows us strategies to approximate solutions. After each class, my mind is buzzing with ideas and strategies.

store.4: I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is the second most challenging for me this semester. It involves a lot of reading, group discussions, and a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself, as we have to collaborate with individuals who have different coding styles and ideas about the final product. This is a great opportunity to learn how to integrate code with others, handle concurrency issues, and manage node failures. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in a config file. However, once we fixed that issue and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.

store.6: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which is a must-take for me as a gamer at heart. The professor is from the industry and has worked on indie games that gained traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even user experience design. The assignments are super creative, and I had a blast designing a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept. The challenge was balancing the difficulty curve to prevent players from getting frustrated and quitting. It was rewarding to see the design come together successfully.

store.8: I initially thought I might regret taking the Introduction to Quantum Computing class, but now I actually enjoy it. The professor's approach focuses on conceptual understanding rather than pure math, which makes it more accessible. We learn about linear algebra, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not building actual quantum computers, but we're exploring algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing to see how quantum computing can revolutionize problem-solving.

store.10: The Capstone Project course is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, API building, front-end interface, and ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to stay organized. Each week, we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and agile practices. It's a lot, but if we can successfully complete this project, I'll be incredibly proud.

store.12: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind, which is my last required non-CS elective. I chose it because it explores interesting connections between consciousness, the concept of mind, and artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have in-depth discussions, which is a welcome change from the coding-intensive nature of my other classes. It's great to analyze abstract ideas and consider the bigger picture, such as the ethical implications of building AI systems that could mimic or simulate human thinking. I recently wrote a paper on whether strong AI could truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a significant topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is crucial, and this course provides valuable perspective.

store.14: My typical college schedule is quite packed. Mondays and Wednesdays are the most hectic days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are slightly lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Thursdays also include Philosophy of Mind in the evening, which can be challenging if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open for working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also make time for undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's fascinating, but it certainly adds to my workload.

store.16: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone consumes around ten hours a week, and it can be even more time-consuming if we encounter major bugs or if the model isn't training properly. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time sink. My group meets at least twice a week to work on these projects. We also rely on Slack and Discord to stay updated and communicate effectively. Coordinating the schedules of five different people can be a logistical nightmare, but despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully immerse myself in purely academic projects, free from the pressures of a job environment.

store.18: I'm having a blast this semester. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but now I've become better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, but it's no longer as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, collaborate effectively, and think critically. These classes are tough, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a great feeling.

store.20: I'm a fourth-year computer science major with a passion for coding. My hobbies help me stay sane amidst a hectic schedule of classes and projects. I believe taking breaks and exploring outside interests is essential for maintaining a fresh perspective in programming.
store.21: Sailing is a hobby that brings me a sense of freedom and challenge. It's a unique activity that allows me to disconnect from the stresses of college life and reconnect with nature. The unpredictability of the wind and the water creates a thrilling puzzle that tests my problem-solving skills. I feel most alive when I'm out on the water, navigating through choppy seas and enjoying the rush of the wind in my face. It's a hobby that I cherish and look forward to whenever I can make time for it.
store.22: Regular gym sessions have become an essential part of my routine. It's a great way to offset the sedentary lifestyle that comes with being a computer science major. I started with a basic lifting routine in my freshman year, and now I aim to hit the gym around four times a week. I'm not looking to become a bodybuilder, but I love seeing the incremental improvements in my strength and energy levels. Working out is also an excellent stress-reliever, especially after long coding sessions. The mental clarity and productivity boost I experience after a good workout are truly remarkable. It's a habit I intend to continue for years to come.
store.23: Gaming is a hobby that complements my interest in technology. I enjoy both PC and console games, but PC gaming is more convenient for me as a CS major. Lately, I've been fascinated by co-op survival games, where I can gather resources, build shelters, and fend off creatures. This genre offers a different kind of problem-solving experience compared to debugging code. I also occasionally participate in fast-paced shooters when friends from class are online and we team up. Gaming is not just a social activity but also a mental challenge for me. I believe gaming can be strategic and collaborative, and it helps me stay connected with others. Additionally, I've experimented with game development using Unity and Unreal Engine, which I'd like to explore further if time allows. The idea of bridging the gap between playing games and creating them is intriguing.
store.24: Reading has been a lifelong passion for me, thanks to my mom's love for literature. She introduced me to fantasy and sci-fi novels when I was a kid, and I'd get lost in other worlds for hours. Even with a busy schedule, I try to squeeze in some reading before bed or on weekends. Lately, I've been fascinated by sci-fi novels that explore artificial intelligence. It's a combination of my academic interests and my curiosity about the future. I enjoy imagining how technology might blur the lines between humans and machines. My current favorite AI-themed sci-fi book is 'The Infinity Courts' by Akemi Dawn Bowman. Reading books like this not only provides relaxation but also helps me explore philosophical questions about the work I'll be doing after graduation. It's a unique way to consider the ethical and social implications of my studies.
store.25: I've found that scheduling my hobbies is key to maintaining a healthy balance. Just like I plan out my study time, I also make time for activities like gym sessions, sailing, gaming, and reading. Sundays are when I usually review my week and decide what I can fit in. If the weather's good, I might head to the gym or rent a dinghy at the local lake. If not, I'll plan an indoor day with friends playing co-op games or working out in my apartment's fitness center. Reading is the easiest to squeeze in – I make sure to read for 30 minutes before bed, which helps me unwind after a long day. By prioritizing these activities, I feel more fulfilled and able to handle the demands of college life.
store.26: I enjoy combining my hobbies to create unique experiences. For example, I've had a day where I spent the morning sailing at the lake, then met up with friends for lunch, and afterwards, we spent the evening playing video games together. It was fascinating to notice how the experience of sailing and coordinating movement in an online co-op shared similarities. In both cases, teamwork, attention to detail, and problem-solving are essential. I love how each hobby, in its own way, demands these skills. It's a great way to appreciate the diversity of my interests and how they complement each other.
store.27: I believe that when you're truly passionate about your hobbies, you'll always find ways to incorporate them into your life, even with a busy schedule. It's not about having hours and hours to devote to each activity, but rather about finding small increments of time that work. For example, I might not be able to read for hours, but I can fit in one chapter before bed. Similarly, I might not be able to sail every weekend, but once a month is doable. And with gaming, even 30 minutes can be enough for a quick match. By being flexible and making the most of the time I have, I'm able to maintain a healthy balance between academics and hobbies.
store.28: I'm glad you have a diverse range of hobbies that bring different aspects of yourself to the table. It's wonderful to have something unique to share beyond coding, which is already a significant part of your life. Your hobbies offer a variety of experiences, from the calming world of reading to the thrilling adventures of sailing, the discipline of weightlifting, and the excitement of co-op games. This diversity makes life more engaging and enjoyable. Thank you for sharing your passions with me – it's been a pleasure to listen!
store.29: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been an eye-opening experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and I'm excited to be a part of it. As a freshman, I didn't initially consider research as an option. I was more focused on coding projects and hackathons. However, one of my professors noticed my ability to combine technical coding with user experience and suggested I apply for a research assistant position in a data visualization lab. I was initially hesitant due to the intimidation factor, but I decided to take the leap. It turned out to be a great decision.
